    Domain knowledge and constraints

    constraints.Rmd

    goal carries soft preferences (“prioritise interpretability”); constraints carry hard requirements that must hold for every final model. Atlas enforces them three ways:

    1. Up front — constraints go into the agent’s task as numbered hard requirements, and the agent is told to design for them from the start (e.g. pick monotone model forms rather than fixing violations later).
    2. During the build — the agent has a check_constraints tool to verify itself before declaring the build done.
    3. After the build — Atlas independently runs every machine check against every model in the results. Violations are sent back to the agent to refit, up to max_fix_rounds times (default 2).

    Three ways to write a constraint 

    library(Atlas)

res <- atlas(mtcars, "mpg", n_models = 2, constraints = list(
  # 1. built-in helpers: machine-checked, model-agnostic
  uses_wt = con_uses("wt"),
  mono_hp = con_monotone("hp", "decreasing"),

  # 2. custom check: any function(model, data) -> TRUE or a violation message
  non_neg = constraint(
    "predicted mpg must never be negative",
    check = function(model, data) {
      p <- predict(model, newdata = data)
      if (all(p >= 0)) TRUE else "some predictions are negative"
    }
  ),

  # 3. plain string: enforced via instructions only (passed = NA in the table)
  no_leak = "qsec is measured after the fact; never use it as a predictor"
))

res$constraints
#>   model constraint passed detail
#>   ...     one row per model x machine-checked constraint ...

    Anything that can be tested in code should get a check; strings are for rules only the agent can honour (like “don’t use this column”). A check may also stop() — errors count as violations, with the message as the detail.

    The built-in helpers

    Both are model-agnostic: they only require predict(model, newdata = <data.frame>) to work, which Atlas tells the agent every final model must support.

    con_uses(var) — the model must actually use a variable. The check scrambles (reverses) the column and compares predictions: if they don’t move, the model isn’t using it. No formula inspection, so it works for any model class and can’t be fooled by wrappers.

    con_monotone(var, direction) — predictions must be monotone in a variable. ICE-style check: for a sample of observed rows, the variable is swept across its observed range with all other predictors held fixed, and every step of every sweep must move in the stated direction (within tol).

    Monotonicity is non-strict, so a model that ignores the variable passes trivially (flat is monotone). That makes it a conditional constraint — “if the model responds to hp, the effect must be decreasing” — without forcing the variable in:

    # monotone if present:
constraints = list(mono_hp = con_monotone("hp", "decreasing"))

# must be used AND monotone:
constraints = list(uses_hp = con_uses("hp"),
                   mono_hp = con_monotone("hp", "decreasing"))

    More custom check patterns 

    # accuracy floor on a reference set
min_r2 <- constraint(
  "in-sample R-squared must be at least 0.7",
  check = function(model, data) {
    r2 <- cor(predict(model, newdata = data), data$mpg)^2
    if (r2 >= 0.7) TRUE else sprintf("R-squared is %.2f", r2)
  }
)

# bounded predictions
in_range <- constraint(
  "predictions must stay within the observed outcome range",
  check = function(model, data) {
    p <- predict(model, newdata = data)
    if (all(p >= min(data$mpg) & p <= max(data$mpg))) TRUE
    else "predictions leave the observed range"
  }
)

# parity across a group
fair_gap <- constraint(
  "mean absolute error must be within 1 unit across am groups",
  check = function(model, data) {
    err <- abs(data$mpg - predict(model, newdata = data))
    gap <- abs(diff(tapply(err, data$am, mean)))
    if (gap <= 1) TRUE else sprintf("MAE gap across am is %.2f", gap)
  }
)

    Excluding features and catching leakage

    Constraints govern how variables are used; exclude removes them entirely — for columns that won’t exist at prediction time in deployment, or that leak the outcome. Excluded columns are dropped from the data before the agent ever sees it, which is a stronger guarantee than any instruction:

    res <- atlas(claims, "severity",
             exclude = c("settlement_amount",   # known after the outcome
                         "claim_ref"))          # ID, useless in deployment

    The surviving predictors are screened automatically with atlas_leakage_screen() — a fast univariate check: any column that alone explains almost all of the outcome (R-squared at/above 0.95) is flagged in the agent’s brief, and the agent must confirm with you that it is genuinely available at prediction time before using it. You can also run the screen yourself before any modeling:

    atlas_leakage_screen(claims, "severity")
#>            variable    r2 flagged
#>   settlement_amount 0.998    TRUE
#>            exposure 0.310   FALSE

    In the app, the “Your data” panel lists every predictor as a checkbox — untick what deployment won’t have — with flagged columns marked “possible leakage” in red.

    Suggested by the agent

    You may forget a monotonicity constraint that’s obviously right for the domain (price should not fall as floor area grows). Atlas is instructed to think about this during data exploration: when it believes a predictor should have a monotone effect, it includes the suggestion — variable, direction, and a one-line why — in the plan it asks you to approve. Each suggestion you approve is added via its add_monotone_constraint tool and becomes a hard, machine-checked constraint, verified and repaired exactly like one you passed yourself (and persisted, so it survives resumes).

    Constraints from natural language

    extract_constraints() parses a plain-language brief into constraint objects, mapping to machine checks wherever it recognises a checkable rule:

    cons <- extract_constraints(
  "weight must be in the model; predictions can never go up as horsepower
   rises; qsec is measured after the fact, never use it",
  data = mtcars
)
cons
#> $uses_wt
#> [machine-checked] The variable `wt` must be used as a predictor.
#> $mono_hp
#> [machine-checked] Predictions must be monotonically decreasing in `hp`.
#> $no_qsec
#> [prompt-only]     Never use qsec as a predictor.

res <- atlas(mtcars, "mpg", constraints = cons)

    The parse is a judgment call, so it returns the list for you to inspect and edit before the build. Passing data lets it validate column names; anything unmappable (unknown column, monotone rule without a direction) falls back to prompt-only enforcement instead of producing a broken check.

    Reading the compliance table

    res$constraints has one row per model x machine-checked constraint, plus one row per prompt-only constraint:

    • passed = TRUE/FALSE — the check ran; detail explains failures.
    • passed = NA — prompt-only: enforced via instructions, not verifiable.

    print(res) shows an UNMET CONSTRAINTS block if anything failed after all repair rounds; a session’s current state can be re-checked any time with res$session$check().
